subsystems.name: Neuron circuit
subsystems.role: mimics a biological neuron: it accumulates input and emits a short voltage pulse (a spike) when a threshold is crossed.

subsystems.name: Synapse array
subsystems.role: stores the weights connecting neurons and multiplies them by incoming spikes.
parts: crossbar of resistive memory cells (RRAM or phase-change)

subsystems.name: Weight memory
subsystems.role: holds learned weights next to the computing cells, avoiding a trip to external DRAM.

subsystems.name: Event router
subsystems.role: sends spikes only to the neurons that need them, as small data packets.

subsystems.name: Plasticity engine
subsystems.role: updates weights as the chip runs, using rules that depend on spike timing.

subsystems.name: Sensors and I/O
subsystems.role: feeds the chip from event-based sensors, which report only changes rather than full frames.

buildSteps.title: Choose the neuron model
buildSteps.detail: Designers pick a mathematical model — usually leaky integrate-and-fire — and decide what must be analogue and what must be digital.

buildSteps.title: Design the synapse crossbar
buildSteps.detail: A grid of memory cells is laid out so a spike travelling along a row is multiplied by each stored weight and summed on a column wire, the same way a biological synapse adds charge.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the memory cells
buildSteps.detail: Resistive or phase-change cells are fabricated in the back-end wiring layers above standard CMOS, so memory and logic sit on one die. Device-to-device variation must be kept low, because the weights are physical conductances.

buildSteps.title: Tape out at a foundry
buildSteps.detail: The digital neuron logic and routers are made on a mature CMOS node, then the memory layers are added; each layer needs its own masks and process calibration.

buildSteps.title: Test and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Every chip is measured, and on-chip or host software trims the conductance of each cell to compensate for manufacturing spread and temperature drift.

buildSteps.title: Package and stack
buildSteps.detail: Multiple dies are bonded together and connected to event sensors, often in a single module for edge devices.

buildSteps.title: Map the network
buildSteps.detail: A compiler places neurons on cores, routes the spike traffic and quantises the trained weights into the analogue cells' usable range — usually the hardest step engineering-wise.

buildSteps.title: Train and deploy
buildSteps.detail: The network is trained (often conventionally, then converted), loaded onto the chip, and fine-tuned on-device with the plasticity circuits.

prerequisites.why: weights are stored as physical resistance, so device spread directly becomes computational error.

prerequisites.tech: Mature CMOS with back-end memory layers
prerequisites.why: every design so far is standard silicon with added resistive memory or pure digital neuron cores.
the power advantage only appears when the input is already sparse spikes rather than video frames.
standard deep-learning training assumes continuous numbers, not discrete spikes in time.
mapping a neural network onto thousands of cores without wasting them is still largely manual.

pathway.milestone: research chips and first commercial edge parts — IBM's TrueNorth, Intel's Loihi line, Manchester's SpiNNaker, and low-power inference chips aimed at always-on sensing
pathway.unlocks: real workloads at microwatt-to-milliwatt power budgets where conventional accelerators are wasteful.

pathway.milestone: hybrid systems where an analogue in-memory array handles matrix work alongside digital logic
pathway.unlocks: in-memory computing for ordinary AI, which is a large market even before spiking models mature.

pathway.milestone: on-chip learning that works reliably across temperature and ageing
pathway.unlocks: devices that adapt in the field instead of being retrained in a data centre.

pathway.milestone: large brain-scale systems with sparse, event-driven communication
pathway.unlocks: always-on perception and robotics at a tiny fraction of today's energy per operation — the main prize, and the one still furthest away.
